title: Where does Father Christmas come from?
subtitle: Sixteen centuries of legend
subject: mythologie
description: A Greek bishop of the 3rd century, a Dutch rider, a New York poem, a newspaper cartoonist and an advertising campaign. Santa Claus was not born, he was assembled piece by piece.
author: angela-bouma

hero.hook: He was not born. He was built, piece by piece, over sixteen centuries.

blocks.text: A Greek bishop, a pagan benefactor and an advertising illustration blend together to shape Santa Claus. It all begins with [[Nicholas of Myra]], born in **270**, a bishop who gives his personal wealth to those who need it most. He becomes the [[patron saint]] of children and sailors.

Over the next **1,600 years**, the legend takes shape. The midwinter customs of Northern Europe bring families together to celebrate and feast. A sleigh, **eight reindeer**, a trip down the chimney: a poem shapes the way people wait for the season. Then an advertising campaign packages the legend as a product. The result is the Santa Claus everyone knows.

In the Netherlands, [[Sinterklaas]] rides through the towns on a **white horse**, wearing a miter and red robes and carrying a staff. Children leave their shoes out with carrots and hay for his horse. The tradition travels to America, where Sinterklaas slowly becomes **Santa Claus**.

blocks.caption: Sinterklaas on his white horse, in red miter and cope, arriving in a Dutch town.

blocks.text: The English have their own midwinter visitor. Clad in fur and jolly as can be, [[Father Christmas]] brings the feasting. He personifies the joy and celebrations of the season, and he goes back to at least the **15th century**. In this version, he has no gifts for the children. English colonists carry him to America, where he takes root alongside Sinterklaas.

In **1823**, a poem published anonymously in New York State, *A Visit from St. Nicholas*, gives Santa Claus his most recognizable form: a sleigh, eight reindeer, and the idea that he comes down the chimney on a snowy night to leave gifts. [[Clement Clarke Moore]] is credited as the author, but the question is still debated.

blocks.caption: A Santa Claus dressed in fur, as in the 1823 poem: photograph taken in New York State around 1872.

blocks.text: From **1863**, the cartoonist [[Thomas Nast]] adds to the portrait in his illustrations for *Harper's Weekly*. He gives him his round belly, his white beard and his **North Pole** workshop. To draw today's Santa Claus, Nast takes both Sinterklaas and Father Christmas as his guides.

From **1931**, Coca-Cola's illustrated advertising campaigns, drawn by the artist [[Haddon Sundblom]], establish the warm, grandfatherly Santa recognizable today: white beard, big belly, belt and suspenders. The company does not invent Santa Claus. It helps standardize his image, the same everywhere, year after year.
The red suit is not a Coca-Cola idea. Thomas Nast was already drawing Santa Claus in red, long before the company's first campaign.

blocks.caption: A Santa Claus at Eaton's department store in Montreal, surrounded by children, in the mid-20th century.

blocks.text: By the mid-**20th century**, department stores, radio specials and movies bring together the legacies of Sinterklaas, the English Father Christmas and Nast's drawings. The result is a single global figure, known by different names in different countries but instantly recognizable everywhere.

sections.title: A legend written by many hands

blocks.text: The story of Santa is not unique. Holidays and folk heroes are made the same way. Through **trade** and contact with other groups, ideas travel and change. A religious tradition slips into an older seasonal festival. The next generation adds its own version, adapted to its needs.

blocks.text: Each new meeting of cultures adds to the story and changes the faces of its characters. No single civilization owns these figures: they belong to human culture as a whole. Santa Claus is a celebration of what happens, over **1,600 years**, when peoples meet and share a holiday.
Greek bishop, Dutch rider, jolly English reveler, poem, press drawings and advertising: Santa Claus is a legend written by many hands over sixteen centuries.
